units.title: Area of Study 1: Recording and production techniques

outcomes.text: Use core and advanced functions of a digital audio workstation.
Identify and use hardware: microphones, audio interfaces, pre-amps, DI boxes, mixing desks, outboard effects, guitar pedals, controller keyboards.
Describe other programming environments such as MIDI or OSC and the impact of new software on production.
Set gain structure to maximise signal-to-noise ratio and avoid clipping, interference and hiss.
Use pre-amp controls: phantom power, gain, pad, high-pass filter, polarity, clip LED.
Compare dynamic, condenser and ribbon microphones.
Compare polar patterns, proximity effect, frequency and transient response, and sensitivity.
Choose microphone distance, angle and multi-mic setups, and manage spill, background noise and plosives.
Explain coincident and spaced stereo pairs and phase relationships between microphones.
Explain how microphones work: diaphragms, electromagnetic induction, capacitance, switches and accessories.
Select and mix waveforms, noise, LFOs, filters and envelopes to create sounds.
Explain how cut-off, resonance and ADSR envelope shape timbre.
Use oscillator tuning, pitch bend, mono and polyphonic modes, portamento and arpeggiator.
Edit samples by cutting, trimming and tuning, and map pitch across the keyboard.
Loop samples using loop points, zero crossings and cross-fades.
Use advanced sampling: sample rate, bit depth, reversing, key zones, velocity layering, time-stretch and synthesis parameters.
Input notes in real time with a controller and in non-real time with a step grid or pencil tool.
Quantise with hard values, swing, snap/grid and groove templates.
Edit in piano roll and list editors: velocity, note length, cutting, looping, duplicating.
Explain how MIDI data works, including controllers, pitch bend and tempo data.
Truncate audio with split tools and set lead-in and lead-out times.
Remove clicks, hiss, hum and plosives, with fades and cross-fades.
Explain how clicks and noises arise, such as discontinuous waveforms.
Use editing functions such as normalising and inverting waveforms.

topics.title: 1.7 Pitch and rhythm correction and manipulation

outcomes.text: Correct pitch with automatic tuning or manual pitch shifting, and use tuning creatively.
Correct rhythm by cutting and moving notes or audio quantise.
Use control parameters: response time, formant shift, cents, polyphonic retuning, transient detection, time-stretch.
Automate volume and pan for fades and stereo movement.
Automate plug-in parameters such as filter cut-off and delay feedback.
Decide when to use a compressor or gate, and explain limiting, expansion, de-essing and pumping.
Set compressor threshold, ratio, make-up gain, attack, release, knee and side-chain.
Set gate threshold, range, attack, release, hold and side-chain, and draw compression and gate graphs.
Set and identify pan positions for tracks in a mix.
Explain panning law, mono-summing, stereo widening, mono compatibility and mid-side processing.
Use shelf, band, low-pass, high-pass and band-pass EQ, parametric and graphic.
Correct sibilance, noise and resonance with EQ.
Explain how gain, frequency, Q, slope and resonance change sound, and draw EQ graphs.
Set wet/dry, bypass, sends and inserts for effects.
Describe reverb types and settings: room, hall, plate, spring, gated, reversed, reverb time, pre-delay, damping.
Describe delay types and settings: multi-tap, slapback, ping pong, delay time, feedback, ADT.
Describe modulated delay (flange, chorus, phaser) with LFO rate, depth, feedback and comb filtering.
Use wah-wah, distortion, overdrive, fuzz and amp modelling parameters.
Use tremolo, vocoder, talk box, and lo-fi effects such as bit-crushing and vinyl crackle.
Set the relative balance of parts.
Explain how compression, EQ and effects change blend.
Use limiting to raise perceived volume.
Apply mastering parameters: limiter gain, fades, stereo width, master reverb mix.
Use master EQ, such as high-shelf boost and rumble filter.

units.title: Area of Study 2: Principles of audio and sound technology

outcomes.text: Explain how room size, absorption, reflection and diffusion affect recordings, including isolation booths.
Describe reverb tail, pre-delay, early and late reflections, RT60 and resonant frequencies.
Describe the frequency ranges of tweeters, woofers and subwoofers.
Explain how monitor speakers work by electromagnetic induction.
Explain how checking mixes on headphones, different speakers and subwoofer systems affects translation.
Compare balanced and unbalanced connections, and use balanced leads to avoid hiss, hum and rumble.
Trace signal path through aux sends, inserts, sub-groups and channel strips.
Compare jack, XLR, MIDI, digital and computer data (USB, Firewire) leads, and DI boxes.
Explain impedance and mic, line and instrument signal levels.
Compare digital and analogue frequency response, dynamic range, headroom and clipping, and the effect of valves and transistors.
Explain A/D and D/A conversion, sample rate, bit depth, bit rate, PCM and compressed formats such as mp3.
Read and draw waveforms, EQ curves, compressor responses, envelopes, frequency and polar response graphs.
Use units: decibels, hertz, milliseconds and note values, bpm, feet, semitones, cents, percentages; use binary and logarithms.
Calculate frequency, phase and amplitude of sound waves.
Manage levels to prevent distortion and maximise signal-to-noise ratio.
Use decibel scales and know when to use peak and RMS metering; explain psycho-acoustics of perceived volume.

units.title: Area of Study 3: The development of recording and production technology

outcomes.text: Compare digital and analogue recording, and the pros and cons of digital hardware and software.
Explain GUIs, sampling theory and converters.
Describe digital sequencing and DAW functions: real-time processing, software instruments, non-destructive editing, convolution reverb, amp modelling.
Describe digital consumer formats (CD, mp3, high-definition masters) and bit rate.
Describe digital multitrack and early sampling hardware with limited memory.
Compare analogue with digital recording, including valves, soft clipping, tape saturation and transistor distortion.
Describe tape machines, editing and splicing, and multitrack tape formats.
Describe analogue consumer formats (vinyl, cassette), mono and stereo releases, and mixing and mastering for them.
Describe analogue effects: tape and bucket-brigade delay, plate and spring reverb, Leslie cabinet, vinyl scratching, pitch changes by tape and vinyl.
Describe analogue synthesisers, modules and patching.
Describe early electric instruments: electric guitar, bass, theremin, Mellotron, electric organ, electric piano, Clavinet.
Place production practice in eras from direct-to-tape mono (1930s) through multitrack to digital and DAWs.
Know the instruments, sounds and ensembles of jazz, blues, rock 'n' roll, rock, metal, punk, soul, disco, funk and reggae.
Know the instruments, sounds and ensembles of acoustic and folk, commercial pop, urban, electronic and dance, music for media, and game and film.
Capture sound accurately and produce a balanced final stereo mix.
Compose to a brief with synthesis, sampling, automation and musical elements such as structure, timbre, texture, harmony and rhythm.
Identify and evaluate production techniques and effect settings in unfamiliar commercial recordings.
Edit, correct, process and mix supplied audio and MIDI, and justify parameter decisions.
